# CHAPTER 362

## THE LOOKOUT

I became a lookout because Tavi wanted to see a fish fly.

This was not a metaphor.

Carrow had actual flying fish.

Apparently nobody had considered telling me.

"They're not fish," Lyssa said.

Tavi was standing on a chair at breakfast, which meant Cala had already told him to sit down at least once.

"They are," he said.

"They're river kites."

"Kites aren't alive."

"Those are."

"Then fish."

"That is not how categories work."

I looked at Cala.

"What are river kites?"

She looked surprised.

"You don't know?"

"I have successfully not known for nineteen years."

"They come through lower spill after first warm rain."

"Doing what?"

Tavi answered before she could.

"Flying."

Useful.

Cala said, "Gliding. Mostly."

Lyssa tore bread.

"Jump from water, catch the lift off spill channels, land upriver."

I stopped eating.

"Why?"

Three people looked at me.

Not because question was stupid.

Because apparently this was childhood knowledge.

Tavi said, "Because they're fish."

That explained nothing and satisfied him completely.

"Breeding run," Cala said. "Or feeding. Depends who you ask."

Better.

"Magical?"

Lyssa shrugged.

"A little."

Carrow's relationship with magic remained offensive.

A little.

Like seasoning.

"How little?"

Cala pointed spoon at me.

"You can go look without making it work."

I had been known too long.

Tavi bounced on chair.

"We have to go before second bell because Naro said they were already at lower gates and if we miss them then they go past mill turn and you can't see them good because roofs and also his brother said one hit a woman in face last year but he lies sometimes, except maybe not about fish because why would you lie about fish when real fish already fly?"

There.

Tavi speech had become a cart rolling downhill.

I liked it.

"Who is Naro?" I asked.

"Naro."

"Excellent."

Cala said, "Boy two doors east."

"I know his mother," Lyssa said.

"Do I?"

"No."

Good.

I finished breakfast.

Eight copper stayed in purse.

No work scheduled.

No reason not to go watch magical fish make poor decisions.

Tavi was already at door.

"Shoes," Cala said.

He looked down.

Bare feet.

"I knew."

"Then do it."

He ran upstairs.

Lyssa said, "You taking him?"

"Apparently."

"I was asking Cala."

Cala said, "Greg can."

I looked between them.

"Interesting transfer of authority."

"Bring him back," Cala said.

"Alive?"

She looked at me.

"Greg."

"Alive."

Tavi returned with shoes on wrong feet.

I pointed.

He looked.

"They still fit."

"That is not the standard."

He changed them while standing.

Nearly fell.

Caught wall.

I waited.

"Sit," I said.

"I can do it."

"You demonstrated. Sit."

He sat.

Shoes corrected.

We left.

I had taken Tavi places before.

Not often enough to have system.

Enough to know children did not move through city like adults.

Adults selected destination and route.

Children selected every object between destination and route.

A blue bottle cap.

A dog with one white ear.

A chalk circle somebody had drawn around a drain.

A man carrying six chairs.

"Why six?"

"Maybe he needs six chairs."

"But why all now?"

"Because carrying one six times is worse."

"What if he drops them?"

"Then carrying one six times becomes competitive."

Tavi watched man until corner hid him.

Then ran three steps to catch up.

"Walking," I said.

"I am."

"That was running."

"Only little."

"Still running."

"You can't run."

I looked at him.

He looked at my crutches.

Not insult.

Observation.

"Correct."

"Can you run with those?"

"Badly."

"Show me."

"No."

"Why?"

"Because I enjoy having teeth."

He considered.

"You could run without falling."

"Probably."

"Then show me."

"No."

"Why?"

This was going well.

Lower spill sat beyond dye lanes where two old water channels came down from east cut and split around a wedge of warehouses.

I had crossed upper bridges.

Never stood at lower gates during fish season.

Apparently season was three mornings long some years and ten days others.

Nobody agreed.

Crowd told me we had found it before water did.

Families lined stone rail.

Children on shoulders.

Vendors with hot buns and paper cones of salted seeds.

Two city workers in green vests had roped off the lowest ledge.

Not because fish were dangerous.

Because people were idiots near moving water.

Comforting.

Tavi stopped.

"There."

I saw nothing.

Then water exploded.

A silver shape came out of spill channel at an angle no fish had business attempting.

Longer than my hand.

Flat fins snapped wide.

Not wings.

Close enough to offend taxonomy.

Blue-white lines lit along its sides.

It climbed.

Actually climbed.

Not much.

Maybe ten feet above water.

Then glided across lower basin, curved in air, and hit upper channel with a splash.

Crowd cheered.

I stared.

Tavi looked at me with enormous satisfaction.

"Fish."

"Fine."

"Say it."

"Fish."

"Flying fish."

"River kite."

"Greg."

"You sound like Lyssa."

"Flying fish."

Another launched.

Then three.

One failed badly and slapped sideways into stone lip before flopping back into current.

Nobody gasped.

It recovered.

Tried again twenty seconds later.

Successful.

I loved it immediately.

Not because artifact.

Not because useful.

Because world had apparently hidden ridiculous fish from me and expected me to accept this.

Blue-white side lines brightened only during air phase.

Maybe field interaction.

Maybe body-generated lift.

Maybe something in water.

I stopped.

Cala's spoon pointed at me in memory.

You can go look without making it work.

Fine.

I looked.

Tavi squeezed between two adults toward rail.

I caught back of his shirt.

"No."

"I can see."

"From here."

"People are tall."

"Cruel world."

"I can't see."

That was true.

Crowd had thickened.

I looked around.

There was a low freight step beside warehouse wall, maybe a foot high.

Bad for me.

Good for him.

Also crowded.

A stack of empty produce crates sat farther back.

Absolutely not.

Tavi saw them same moment.

"I can stand on those."

"No."

"They're strong."

"No."

"You didn't check."

"I checked spiritually."

"That's not checking."

Damn child.

A woman beside us laughed.

She had a baby tied against chest and a girl maybe eight holding sleeve.

"He's right," she said.

"Please don't strengthen him."

"Sorry."

She was not sorry.

Tavi pointed at her.

"She says."

"She is not in charge of you."

Woman said, "Definitely not."

Good.

A city worker moved along rope.

"Keep children behind yellow stones. No crates, no rail sitting. If you need a viewing step, west wall has public blocks."

There.

Infrastructure defeated improvisation.

"Public blocks," I said.

Tavi groaned like government had ruined childhood.

We moved west.

Public blocks were three broad stone risers built into wall.

Not seating exactly.

Viewing steps.

Children occupied most.

Parents behind.

I found Tavi space on lowest block.

"Stay on this one."

"Second is better."

"Lowest."

"Why?"

"Because I can reach you without climbing."

He looked at my leg.

Then at step.

"Okay."

No argument.

That landed strangely.

Not pity.

Geometry.

He climbed lowest block and immediately forgot me because six fish launched together.

For ten minutes I was not Greg the collector or model or reader or whatever else city had temporarily named me.

I was an adult standing behind a child at water.

This turned out to involve more work than expected.

"Don't lean."

"I'm not."

"Your entire body is past your feet."

"But I'm not falling."

"That is a temporary success condition."

"Look!"

I looked.

A fish came high.

Higher than others.

Blue-white side light bright enough to see in daylight.

It crossed over rope line.

Over crowd.

People ducked.

The fish did not.

It hit canvas awning over seed vendor.

THUMP.

Canvas sagged.

Fish flopped once.

Vendor shouted something impolite.

Then fish slid down canvas, launched off edge somehow, and smacked a man in shoulder.

Crowd erupted.

Man caught fish reflexively.

This was wrong move.

The side lines flashed.

His hair lifted straight up.

He yelled and dropped it.

Fish hit street, flopped twice, then skitter-glided under rope and back into water.

Tavi was vibrating.

"Naro didn't lie!"

"About woman in face?"

"Fish hit man. Same."

"Those are different people and body parts."

"But fish hit."

Fair.

Green-vest worker shouted, "Do not catch kites! Let them fall!"

The vendor was inspecting awning.

Man's hair slowly lowered.

No injury beyond dignity.

Good.

Tavi turned to me.

"If one hits us, can I touch it?"

"No."

"What if it can't get back?"

"Worker."

"What if worker isn't there?"

"We find one."

"What if all workers leave?"

"Why would all workers leave during fish?"

"Maybe lunch."

"Then fish have won."

He accepted this.

Crowd shifted.

Somebody behind us said, "Big run coming."

I looked toward lower channel.

Water had changed.

Not level.

Texture.

Silver flashes beneath surface.

Dozens.

Maybe more.

Blue-white light flickered under water like broken reflection.

Workers started moving.

Not panic.

Procedure.

"Children down one step," one called. "Keep west lane open. Big run."

Parents repeated it.

Children complained.

Tavi stayed lowest already.

Good decision paid dividends.

I moved closer behind him.

Not touching.

Ready.

First wave launched.

Eight.

Ten.

Hard to count.

Then second.

The air over basin filled with silver bodies.

Some low.

Some high.

Blue-white lines made arcs.

Not organized.

Not school formation.

Chaos with direction.

Every fish wanted upstream and possessed a different opinion about route.

People shouted.

Laughed.

Duck calls moved through crowd.

One fish clipped rope post.

Another landed in empty bun basket and immediately left.

Tavi screamed with joy.

Then he stepped down.

Not toward water.

Sideways.

Following one fish that had landed behind viewing blocks.

I caught shoulder.

"Stay."

"It can't get up."

Fish flopped against wall.

Blue lines flashed.

No clear path to water because crowd feet.

Tavi pulled against my hand.

"Greg."

"Stay."

"It'll die."

Not mine anymore.

Household absorbed benefit without ledger.

I went upstairs.

Eight copper.

Twenty-six Vale.

No bit accounting.

No mana.

One practical artifact use.

I opened notes.

This time I did write artifact result because unlike fish, this was mine and heat could hurt somebody.

THREE REEDS

SECOND LIGHT CONTEXT: ORDINARY OIL LAMP / SEPARATE / UNMOUNTED

FACED WEST WINDOW

VISIBLE STRAY WASH AT WINDOW REDUCED

MAIN TABLE LIGHT REMAINED USABLE

OFF = WINDOW SPILL RETURNED

REAR PLATE WARMED QUICKLY AGAIN

NO SAFE DURATION ESTABLISHED

EMBERWINGS THINNED DURING USE / DO NOT CLAIM CAUSE

Then:

PRACTICAL ANSWER WAS BAKING TRAY.

I stared at that.

Five copper artifact defeated by kitchen equipment.

No.

Wrong frame.

Artifact had done exactly what I bought it hoping it might do.

It controlled where light leaked.

That mattered.

Then a cheaper object was enough for this specific problem.

Also mattered.

Owning tool did not mean every problem deserved tool.

Too wise again.

Better.

From two doors east, somebody shouted.

Naro, probably.

Then Mevi shouted back.

Normal.

Had not been technician.

Had not been hero.

Brought something useful.

Neighbor.

Vale found me through bread.

Efficient.

TOMORROW / THIRD BELL

No purchase.

"Greg."

"No."

"No."

Not special.

Correct answer.

Not promise against universe.

"Bring this. East Annex, not main office. Third bell."

"Where?"

She gave directions.

I left.

No drama.

No hidden trap.

Debt could simply be work.

That was almost more unsettling.

I spent rest of day not preparing for paper.

This required discipline.

Tavi asked what job was.

"Looking at numbers."

"You do that at home free."

"I have been exploited."

Cala said, "By yourself."

"Worst employer."

Lyssa was trimming thread ends from a finished cuff.

She looked at me.

"Yes."

"Good."

Just good.

That landed.

Next morning I went East Annex.

No artifacts beyond oval in normal shoulder bag.

No Three Reeds.

No holdfast.

No rest stone.

Eight copper stayed home except ordinary carry coin I did not count because bit continuity remained a problem nobody in world knew existed.

I disliked that sentence immediately.

Not because of money.

Because I had started thinking like ledger.

East Annex sat behind old court buildings where streets narrowed and walls became older than signs attached to them.

Three-story stone building.

Small windows.

Iron shutters open for morning.

Vale mark over door, older style than main office.

Thin hair.

"Yes."

Role supplied.

Good beginning.

TRANSFER

HOLD

A pencil.

Magical office equipment.

Naturally.

"Hold."

"Damaged?"

"Hold."

"Unreadable?"

"Hold."

Professionally.

Account mark.

Shelf code.

Page range.

Private enough to matter.

Boring enough to protect.

E-14-77

pages 1 through 6.

E-14-77

1-6.

Next.

E-14-81.

Pages 1-4.

Match.

Transfer.

Stamp.

E-14-83.

Pages 1-9.

He took bundle.

Did not open.

Placed HOLD.

"Good."

No investigation.

Next.

Paper work had rhythm.

Not exciting rhythm.

But satisfying.

Read.

Compare.

Move.

Pause.

Stamp.

Blue flash.

The magical stamp was probably some registry-authentication device.

I did not ask.

Growth again.

"Double mark."

"Cause?"

"Greg."

"Stopping."

He almost smiled.

Dialogue victory.

My back wanted different chair.

I shifted.

Orsen noticed.

"Break?"

"Two minutes."

He nodded.

I stood.

Hands stretched.

Right leg loosened.

No issue.

Across room two other clerks worked with larger ledgers.

One woman had tiny brass page-weight that crawled itself half inch whenever she turned page.

Then away.

Not everything magical needed me.

This city was becoming increasingly inconsiderate about that.

Not dramatic.

Water stain along lower edge.

Page range maybe complete.

Hold.

Hold.

"Hold."

Dark blue outer coat.

Silver buttons.

No obvious artifact.

Front clerk pointed toward Orsen.

She came over.

Orsen's posture changed.

Not fear.

Formality.

"Mistress Ceral."

"Orsen. I need transfer copy for Morrow account block."

She gave one.

I kept eyes on my sheet.

Private account.

Not mine.

Orsen checked shelf list.

Her voice tightened.

His did not.

Different war.

M-22-11.

Her gaze dropped to crutches.

Good.

Usually.

Because Lyssa could carry cloth herself.

Lyssa said, "Okay. First lot."

Marra held out hand.

Lyssa shook it.

I did not.

Not my deal.

That distinction felt better than expected.

I left for house.

On route I realized I had become errand boy.

Partner had lasted seventeen minutes.

Roles were flexible.

At home Cala was still at table.

Tavi gone outside with explicit permission, apparently.

"She took it?" Cala asked.

"First lot. Six copper if accepted. Four days. She's using rear bench today for two bits."

Cala nodded once.

Not shocked.

"Good."

"She wants shears, yellow needle roll, pressing cloth, food."

"She said yellow?"

"Yes."

"Good. Blue has coarse needles."

Useful.

I went upstairs.

Left drawer.

Two rolls.

Yellow.

Blue.

I took yellow.

Shears in leather sleeve.

Pressing cloth behind stove downstairs.

Cala wrapped bread, cheese, apple.

"For both?"

"She said food."

"Take enough for both."

"I wasn't invited to work."

"You will be there at midday."

This was household logistics, not prophecy.

She was right.

I carried everything back in shoulder bag.

Marra's rear workroom was hotter now.

Two pressing irons sat near small stove.

Lyssa had first apron pieces laid out.

Jessa occupied opposite bench with dark green sleeve guards.

I handed tools.

Lyssa checked yellow roll.

"You listened."

"Occasionally."

"Food?"

I held bag.

"Cala assumed I also eat."

"Smart woman."

Marra called from front, "Don't put food on work bench."

Lyssa called back, "I know."

Jessa said, "She says it because Fera did."

"I don't care why she says it."

"There was mustard."

Lyssa stopped.

"On cloth?"

"White cuff."

"Why was Fera eating mustard near white cuff?"

Jessa spread hands.

"Now you understand why you're less annoying."

Different register.

Longer gossip.

Good.

I could leave.

I probably should.

Lyssa threaded needle.

Then said, without looking up, "You can stay for lunch."

"Furniture?"

"Lunch furniture."

I stayed.

Not all afternoon.

That mattered too.

I watched first seam because she asked me to check whether cloth bundle at table edge blocked walkway for my crutches.

It did.

We moved it.

Then I sat by wall and read an old public broadsheet somebody had left on chair.

No investigation.

Mostly shipping notices and argument about canal toll.

Lyssa worked.

Her speech changed when hands busy.

Less dry.

More muttering.

"No, that's stupid. Why would you put notch there? Fine. Fine, I see why. Still ugly. Jessa, is this quarter turn or half?"

"Half on brown. Quarter on gray."

"Card says quarter."

"Old card."

Lyssa stopped.

"Marra."

Marra came.

They corrected card.

No secret test this time.

Good.

At lunch we sat on back step.

Lyssa ate apple first.

"You think I should've taken it?"

There.

Permission.

"Yes."

"Why?"

"First lot is bounded. Materials supplied. Six copper is meaningful. You paid two bits to learn pace before bringing rest home. You kept penalty off first lot. And you can still hate it after four days."

She chewed.

"Too many reasons."

"You asked."

"I know."

"Also Marra clearly wants you because you're good."

She looked away.

Not embarrassed exactly.

Something adjacent.

"She wants cheap finishing."

"Also true."

She looked back.

"See, that's why I ask you."

"Because I ruin compliment?"

"Because you don't make me choose between compliment and math."

That was better than compliment.

I ate bread.

"Six isn't shop rate," I said.

"No."

"But you aren't paying materials or shop overhead except today bench."

"No."

"How many hours?"

"Don't know yet. That's why today."

"Then today matters."

"Yes."

She leaned back against wall.

"If it takes me four full days, six is bad."

"Probably."

"If I can do it around other work in maybe two long days plus pieces, better."

"Yes."

"If second lot is ten and bigger, depends how much bigger."

"Yes."

She frowned.

"You're annoying when agreeing."

"I can disagree randomly."

"Don't."

We ate.

After lunch I left.

No reason to sit there proving support.

That would become surveillance with good intentions.

Lyssa did not ask me to stay.

I did not make her.

At door she said, "Can you tell Cala I might be late?"

"How late?"

"Before dinner. Probably."

"That is not late."

"For starting dinner work it is."

"I'll tell her."

"Thanks."

Then she went back to bench.

I went home.

Cala heard report.

"Good," she said.

"You say good a lot."

"When things are good."

"Disturbing consistency."

She handed me turnips.

"Cut."

Apparently my role changed again.

I cut turnips badly enough that Cala took knife after third.

"Too thick."

"They become thinner when chewed."

"Move."

I moved.

Tavi returned with mud on one knee and no explanation worth believing.

Normal afternoon.

Lyssa came home before dinner.

Tired.

Not miserable.

Important difference.

She dropped into chair.

"Four aprons. Four sleeve pairs."

"Accepted?" Cala asked.

"Marra checked first two of each. Clean. Rest stay until lot return."

"Pace?" I asked.

Lyssa rubbed fingers.

"Better after second. If home setup doesn't fight me, maybe two and half days total work. Spread over four."

"Six still good?"

She thought.

"Good enough to finish first lot."

Not same as yes forever.

Good.

She looked at me.

"You told Cala terms?"

"Only six, four days, supplied materials, two-bit bench today."

"Penalty?"

"No."

"Why?"

"Not household-relevant unless future lot."

She nodded.

Then paused.

"Thank you."

"For carrying cloth?"

"For not making it yours."

That landed harder than six copper.

I covered with stupidity.

"I considered stealing contract."

"You'd sew badly."

"I could learn."

"No."

"Hostile workplace."

She smiled.

Later upstairs I opened notebook.

My own ledger first.

CASH: 8 C

VALE: 23 C

Nothing changed.

Then I almost wrote Lyssa's six-copper job.

Stopped.

Her money.

Her work.

Not my ledger.

I wrote only:

LYSSA / MARRA FIRST LOT

ASK BEFORE ADVICE

IF ASKED TO WITNESS TERMS, REPEAT TERMS

DO NOT BECOME OWNER OF DECISION

Then I stared at last line.

Partner was dangerous word.

People used it to mean business.

Romance.

Work.

Crime.

Cards.

Two people carrying opposite ends of table.

Today it meant simpler thing.

She wanted me beside her while she decided something that belonged to her.

So I stood beside her.

Then I left when she didn't need me.

Partner.

For that.

Enough.
# CHAPTER 366

## THE DANCER

I was invited dancing because somebody hated me.

That was my first theory.

My second was worse.

"You want to go?" Lyssa asked.

She stood by table with hair half tied and charcoal coat open.

No cloth bundle.

No work card.

No emergency.

Suspicious.

"Where?"

"Lantern Court."

I waited.

"For?"

"Music."

"Why?"

She stared at me.

Cala, from stove, said, "Because people go listen to music."

"At home music cannot trample me."

Tavi looked up from floor.

"You can't dance."

There.

Household support.

"I can dance."

"With crutches?"

"I had legs before you were born."

"You have legs now."

"One and a half."

Cala said, "Greg."

"One and some paperwork."

Lyssa laughed.

Tavi looked at my left knee like maybe paperwork lived there.

"Can you?"

Good question.

Could I dance now?

First life, yes.

Not professionally.

Not well enough to impress anyone who mattered.

But enough taverns, festivals, weddings, victory feasts, terrible diplomatic dinners, and one memorable siege-ceasefire where three kingdoms pretended nobody had poisoned a duke.

This body?

Different problem.

"Probably badly," I said.

Lyssa said, "Good."

"That was fast."

"I don't want good dancing. I want to go out."

There.

No productivity.

No contract.

No object.

No money plan.

Just out.

My brain immediately searched for reasons not to.

Crowd.

Uneven paving.

Standing too long.

Crutches around feet.

Unknown dance style.

Possibility of being nineteen in public.

Last one severe.

Lyssa watched all of that happen on my face.

"You can say no."

That made saying no harder.

Not manipulation.

Freedom.

Annoying.

"When?"

"After dinner."

"How long?"

"Greg."

"Reasonable question."

"Until we want to leave."

Terrible answer.

Excellent answer.

"Fine."

Tavi said, "I want to see."

"No," Cala said.

"Why?"

"Because you're staying here."

"Why?"

"Because I said so."

Tavi looked at me.

I looked away.

Not my jurisdiction.

After dinner Lyssa changed nothing except hair.

That surprised me.

I expected some ritual.

Different dress.

Different shoes.

Something.

She wore charcoal coat over ordinary clothes, hair tied back with dark ribbon, boots she already owned.

I wore what I had.

Brown shoulder bag stayed home.

Oval stayed home with it.

That felt strange.

I almost went back for bag.

Then didn't.

No artifact.

No notebook.

No wrapped charcoal.

Just me.

Disgusting.

Lantern Court sat north of market district where three streets widened around old fountain basin that no longer held water.

Tonight it held musicians.

Not literally in basin.

Mostly.

A low platform had been laid across one half.

Five players.

Two hand drums.

Long-necked string instrument.

Short brass horn.

And something like wooden ribs hung from frame, struck with padded sticks.

Each rib glowed faintly when hit.

Not bright.

Amber pulse along grain.

Sound carried farther than it should have.

I noticed.

Then did not investigate.

Growth remained exhausting.

Lanterns hung on cords across court.

Actual lanterns.

No flying fish.

People stood around edges with cups, bread, skewers, folded paper trays.

Center paving mostly clear.

Maybe forty people.

Not formal.

Not performance exactly.

Music for being there.

Lyssa stopped at edge.

"Still want to leave?"

"I never said I wanted to leave."

"Your shoulders did."

I loosened them.

"Traitors."

She smiled.

First song already moving.

Not one I knew.

Pattern simple enough.

Four-beat phrase with third dragged slightly late.

People in center danced mostly in pairs or loose groups.

Steps lateral.

Turn.

Back.

Cross.

Some hand contact.

Some not.

My first-life body supplied six wrong dances immediately.

None useful.

Lyssa said, "Drink?"

"What?"

"You look like you're preparing military campaign."

"Terrain matters."

"It's a courtyard."

"Historically dangerous terrain."

She bought herself something warm from stall.

I did not ask price.

She did not offer me one.

Good.

I stood near low wall where I could lean hip if needed.

We listened through first song.

Then second.

Lyssa moved with music without dancing.

Small shift in shoulders.

Heel tapping.

I watched center.

Not because afraid.

Because information gathering was noble and not cowardice.

An older man danced with woman using cane.

Not same as crutches.

Useful anyway.

She kept cane mostly planted during turns, pivoted around right foot, let partner move more.

Another pair barely moved feet at all.

Just weight shift and hands.

Nobody cared.

That was problem.

If nobody cared, I lost excuse.

Lyssa finished drink.

"Come on."

"No."

She laughed.

"You said yes."

"To going out."

"Correct."

She did not pull me.

She walked into edge of dance space alone.

Then turned around.

Not challenging.

Just there.

I hated this.

I went.

First problem was crutch tips.

Not slipping.

Paving dry.

But people stepped backward without looking.

I kept to outer ring.

Lyssa stood facing me.

"What do I do?"

"You said you could dance."

"I lied under pressure."

"There was no pressure."

"Exactly. More dangerous."

She showed step.

Left.

Together.

Right.

Together.

Small turn on fourth phrase.

I looked down.

"Don't."

"I need feet."

"You know where yours is."

"Optimistic."

"Greg."

I looked up.

We tried.

Left for her meant right for me.

Easy with right foot.

Together meant bring crutches, then body.

Other direction meant left knee and crutch geometry.

No foot to place.

Could shift pelvis over prosthetic absence only in ways this body did not permit because there was no prosthesis.

Permanent BKA knee preserved.

No fake limb.

So standard step broke.

I stopped.

Lyssa stopped.

No pity.

Good.

"Different," she said.

"Profound."

"Can you turn?"

"Yes."

"Show me."

I planted right crutch slightly forward, left crutch wider, right foot pivot.

Quarter turn.

Reset.

Another.

Not fast.

Stable.

Lyssa watched.

"Okay."

She changed her own step.

Not teacher anymore.

Testing shared geometry.

She moved around me on dragged third beat while I shifted weight and pivoted smaller.

Then returned.

"Again."

Again.

This worked.

Barely dance.

Definitely movement.

Third try, I caught rhythm.

Right foot step.

Crutches together.

Weight shift.

Small pivot.

Lyssa crossed past left side instead of expecting me to travel there.

Return.

My shoulders stopped trying to solve.

Music did something irritating.

Body followed.

Not old body.

This one.

That distinction arrived without permission.

I missed beat.

Lyssa said, "There."

"What?"

"You were doing it."

"Then you spoke."

"Sorry."

"Sabotage."

She laughed and nearly stepped on right crutch.

I moved it.

"Danger."

"Your stick attacked me."

"Crutch."

"Aggressive crutch."

We continued.

One song.

Then I stopped.

Not because pain.

Hands tired faster than expected.

Forearms warm.

Right calf doing more than fair share.

"Wall," I said.

Lyssa nodded.

No `are you okay` parade.

We went back to edge.

I leaned.

She stood beside me breathing slightly harder.

"That was dancing," she said.

"Legally?"

"Barely."

"I'll appeal."

A woman near us laughed.

Not at crutches.

At sentence.

She was maybe thirty, broad face, red scarf, holding paper tray of fried roots.

"He'll lose," she told Lyssa.

"I know."

I said, "Corrupt court."

Woman ate root.

"All dance courts corrupt."

Then she walked away.

No introduction.

Perfect stranger interaction.

Third song faster.

We watched.

A group of four took center, spinning in linked pattern.

No chance.

Not yet.

Maybe never.

Fine.

Lyssa said, "You don't have to do every one."

"I know."

"You looked offended."

"By their knees."

"Their knees?"

"Showing off."

She laughed again.

Fourth song slower.

Different pattern.

People paired closer.

Less traveling.

Lyssa looked at me.

I said, "Maybe."

"That's almost enthusiasm."

"Don't ruin it."

We went back.

This time I chose movement first.

No attempt to copy standard lateral step.

Right foot marked beat.

Crutches carried rhythm as much as body.

Tap.

Plant.

Shift.

Pivot.

Lyssa adapted.

Her hands stayed mostly free until she held my forearm once during turn.

Not support.

Contact.

Important difference.

I felt it anyway.

Music changed phrase.

She moved closer.

I moved crutch out before she arrived.

Competence.

Tiny.

Useful.

Then somebody behind me backed into left crutch.

Hard enough to knock tip sideways.

My body reacted before thought.

Right crutch planted.

Right foot loaded.

Left knee lifted clear.

I caught balance.

The man spun around.

"Shit. Sorry. Sorry, I didn't see."

He was young, maybe my age, flushed from dancing.

Hands up.

"I'm good."

"You sure?"

"Yes."

He looked at crutch.

"I kicked it."

"It survived."

"I can get someone."

"For crutch feelings?"

He blinked.

Lyssa said, "He's fine."

"Right. Sorry."

He backed away more carefully.

No fight.

No humiliation.

No public lesson.

Just collision.

My heart had jumped harder than incident deserved.

Body remembered falling better than pride admitted.

Lyssa saw that.

Didn't say it.

She asked, "Wall?"

I considered.

Then shook head.

"Finish song."

Her expression changed.

Small.

Not praise.

Okay.

We finished.

More careful.

Not frozen.

That mattered.

At end I went wall voluntarily.

Hands definitely tired now.

I rubbed palms.

No blister.

No skin issue.

Lyssa leaned beside me.

"Want to leave?"

I looked around.

Lanterns.

Amber ribs pulsing with each struck note.

People talking over music.

Fried-root smell.

A child asleep across someone's shoulders near fountain edge.

Two women arguing whether horn player had skipped verse.

The man who hit my crutch now dancing six feet farther away from everyone.

I smiled.

"Not yet."

Lyssa said nothing.

Good.

We stayed two more songs without dancing.

Then one where she danced with a woman she apparently knew from cloth district.

I had never met her.

Lyssa introduced us only after.

"Greg, Pera. Pera, Greg."

Pera had curls tied in yellow cloth and spoke as if sentences needed extra rooms.

"Oh, you're Greg. I thought you were taller, which is stupid because Lyssa never said tall, she said you use crutches and somehow my brain decided that meant tall, maybe because crutches are long, which makes no sense because then I'd think everyone with broom was tall."

I liked her immediately.

"I am devastated."

"See, that. She said you do that."

Lyssa said, "I did not say that."

"You did. Not those words. You made face."

"What face?"

Pera made an expression that looked like someone smelling competent cheese.

Lyssa stared.

I said, "Accurate."

"Don't encourage her."

Pera pointed at my crutches.

"You danced?"

"Allegedly."

"Good. My uncle dances with one leg and a cane but he cheats because he was already terrible before losing it, so nobody can tell what changed."

Lyssa made choking sound.

I laughed.

Actual laugh.

Pera continued, "He says same thing. Anyway I need water. Bye."

She left.

I looked at Lyssa.

"You have been hiding her."

"For safety."

"Mine or hers?"

"Everyone's."

Good.

Dialogue variance alive.

Last dance we did was not really a dance.

Musicians slowed into closing piece.

People mostly swayed.

Lyssa stood beside me rather than opposite.

I kept right crutch planted, left angled, right foot tapping.

She leaned shoulder lightly into mine.

No turn.

No step pattern.

Just beat.

I could do beat.

First life supplied memories anyway.

A hall with polished floor.

A woman whose name I had forgotten before she died.

A winter festival in capital that no longer existed in same form.

Boots.

Two feet.

No crutches.

Older hands.

Older scars.

Then Lantern Court came back.

Nineteen.

One right foot.

Left knee.

Two crutches.

Lyssa's shoulder.

Amber ribs.

Not replacement.

Nothing replaced anything.

That was childish arithmetic.

This was another thing.

Song ended.

We walked home slowly.

Not because I couldn't faster.

Because neither of us did.

Halfway home Lyssa said, "You liked it."

"Parts."

"You liked it."

"I liked Pera."

"Dangerous."

"I liked fried-root smell."

"You didn't buy any."

"I can appreciate without acquisition."

"Write that down."

"Never."

She bumped my shoulder lightly.

"You danced."

I considered denying.

Didn't.

"Yeah."

At house Cala was awake.

Tavi was not.

"Good?" she asked.

Lyssa said, "He danced."

Cala looked at me.

"Did he?"

"Barely."

"Traitor."

Cala smiled.

"Good."

Of course.

Upstairs I sat on bed and checked hands.

Red pressure marks.

Normal.

Right calf tired.

Shoulders tired.

No injury.

No fall.

No magic.

No money earned.

No debt reduced.

No artifact learned.

No thread resolved.

I had gone somewhere because Lyssa wanted to go.

Then stayed because I wanted to stay.

I almost opened notebook.

Didn't.

Nothing needed recording.

That felt wrong enough to be useful.

I lay back.

Dancer.

Bad one.

Still counted.
# CHAPTER 367

## THE INSTRUCTOR

Jori wanted me to teach three stagehands how not to die.

This was flattering until I met stagehands.

"They're not idiots," she said.

We stood inside theatre side door while rain tapped roof hard enough to make conversation private.

"That is a worrying opening."

"We had two near collisions last week."

"What am I teaching?"

"Moving under bad light."

That was more specific.

Jori pointed toward rehearsal floor.

Theatre had changed since last time.

Not structurally.

People.

A half-painted wall flat leaned near rear rail. Two rope coils sat on marked boards. Someone had chalked three pale lanes across floor from wings to center and then erased half of one badly.

Nessa stood on ladder adjusting hood over practice lamp.

Not Three Reeds.

Normal theatre equipment.

Good.

"We had two near collisions last week during blackout shift," Jori said. "No injuries. One dropped prop. One person walked into frame because they were watching glow mark instead of route."

"Why me?"

"Because you move with occupied hands and limited step options every day."

I looked at crutches.

"My hands are not occupied. They are infrastructure."

"Fine. Because your infrastructure makes you think about route before moving."

Better.

"And because you noticed rear spill during Three Reeds test before Nessa did."

From ladder Nessa said, "I heard that."

Jori raised voice.

"Good."

Nessa said something rude under breath.

Dialogue alive.

"I am not theatre safety instructor," I said.

"I know."

"I am not rigging specialist."

"I know."

"I am not blackout movement specialist."

Jori looked at me.

"Do you know how to walk through dark room without hitting things?"

"Usually."

"Can you explain why?"

Maybe.

"How much?"

Jori smiled slightly.

There he is.

"Two copper. Two hours. Today. You teach route discipline under low light. I own theatre rules. Nessa owns lamp. You do not certify anyone."

Clear.

"Three people?"

"Three."

"Who?"

"Mett, Olo, Brenna."

Brenna I knew by sight maybe.

Mett maybe not.

Olo definitely not.

No extortion Bren.

Different name.

Thank gods.

"What does success mean?"

Jori's expression changed.

Not annoyed.

Interested.

"They can cross marked route under reduced light, stop on lost orientation instead of guessing, communicate obstruction, and restart from known point."

"Carrying?"

"Empty first. Then one light prop each."

"No speed test."

"Agreed."

"No surprise obstacles."

"Agreed."

"No pretending actual blackout if enough light remains to cheat."

Nessa climbed down.

"That one is mine."

"Can you make it dark enough?"

She looked offended.

"Yes."

"Safely?"

More offended.

"Jori."

Jori said, "He asks everyone like that."

"I dislike him."

"You liked him last time."

"Conditions changed."

I said, "Healthy relationship."

Nessa pointed at me.

"Two hours. Then leave."

Good.

I accepted.

Two copper mattered.

Not desperate money.

Still money.

Cash would go eight to ten if paid.

Vale stayed twenty-three.

Different stair.

The three stagehands arrived together.

Mett was broad, maybe twenty-five, hair shaved at sides, talked before fully entering room.

"Jori said this isn't a test, which means it is probably a test in the way people say something isn't a test right before they remember it later when deciding whether you get shifts."

Jori said, "It isn't a test."

Mett nodded.

"Exactly."

Brenna was older than me by maybe ten years, narrow face, sleeves rolled unevenly, expression skeptical.

Olo was younger, maybe seventeen, tall and quiet enough that silence itself seemed intentional.

Three different problems already.

I stood at chalk line.

"I'm Greg."

Mett said, "We know."

Brenna said, "He knows. I know you have crutches. That's different."

Olo said nothing.

Excellent.

"Jori hired me for two hours to teach route discipline under low light. I am not grading you. I am not certifying you. If Jori secretly grades you afterward, haunt her."

Jori, behind me, said, "Useful opening."

"I establish trust."

"Poorly."

Mett raised hand.

"Can we haunt while employed?"

"Advanced course."

Brenna almost smiled.

Good.

I pointed to chalk route.

"Show me how you cross now. Full light."

Mett went first.

Fast.

Too fast.

He looked at destination, not floor.

Fine in full light.

Brenna slower, checked edges, stepped around rope coil even though outside route.

Olo followed chalk exactly.

Exactly enough to be problem.

At erased section he hesitated, then guessed where line continued.

There.

Three habits.

"Again," I said.

Mett groaned.

"Already?"

"We have achieved repetition."

"I hate training."

"Useful information."

Second crossing I stopped each at midpoint.

"Where is nearest known boundary?"

Mett looked around.

"Wing post."

Brenna said, "Rear rail."

Olo pointed at chalk under foot.

"That isn't boundary," I said.

He looked at me.

"It's route."

"What if mark disappears?"

He shrugged.

First words came quiet.

"Then I know roughly."

"Roughly is how frame gets forehead."

Brenna said, "That happened to Mett."

Mett touched forehead.

"Once."

"Last week."

"Still once."

Good.

I walked route myself.

Not to demonstrate speed.

Opposite.

"I cannot make lateral correction quickly to left."

I tapped left crutch.

"So before moving I want three things. Start point. Next boundary. Stop condition."

Mett said, "That's very dramatic for twelve steps."

"Twelve steps can still end in wall."

"Fair."

"Start point is where you know you are. Next boundary is something physical or fixed enough to orient from. Stop condition is what makes you stop rather than inventing route."

Brenna crossed arms.

"We have glow marks."

"Good. What happens when prop blocks one?"

"Use next."

"What happens when next is behind you?"

She frowned.

"Then stop."

"Yes."

"That's it?"

"Mostly."

She looked disappointed.

People wanted expertise to be secret.

Usually it was boring things done before panic.

Nessa reduced lamps.

Room dimmed.

Not dark.

Then dimmer.

Amber route marks near floor became visible.

Different from chalk.

Small painted tabs with weak stored glow.

I knew general family.

No need lecture.

"First pass," I said. "No props. No speed. Say boundary before moving."

Mett stared.

"Out loud?"

"Yes."

"This is humiliating."

"Good. Humiliation improves memory."

Jori said, "Not official theatre doctrine."

"Coward."

Mett went.

"Wing post."

Step.

"Low mark."

Step.

"Center seam."

He reached erased-chalk section, but low-light route used glow tab at wall instead.

"Rear lamp bracket."

Better.

Brenna did same with fewer words.

Olo moved too soon after naming mark, before eyes adjusted from brighter wing.

I stopped him.

"Why?"

He looked annoyed.

Good.

"I saw it."

"You saw one thing."

"That's enough."

"No."

Silence.

I knew this kind.

Not stupid.

Hated being corrected in public.

Maybe especially by nineteen-year-old with crutches.

Fair enough.

"Come here," I said.

He did.

I pointed toward route.

"Look at center mark."

He did.

"Now tell me what's left of it."

"Frame."

"Right?"

"Rope."

"Behind?"

He glanced.

"Wing post."

"Now move."

He crossed cleanly.

"You weren't waiting for mark," I said. "You were waiting for room."

He nodded once.

That was enough.

Second pass Nessa reduced light again.

Mett said, "Can she stop doing that?"

Nessa said, "No."

"I respect consistency."

Now room was dark enough that faces became suggestions.

Glow marks stronger by contrast.

Jori stayed near wall.

I heard her more than saw.

"Carry props," she said.

Three objects waited.

Wooden bowl.

Rolled cloth.

Light frame corner.

Mett took bowl.

Brenna cloth.

Olo frame.

"No," I said.

Olo stopped.

"Why?"

"Frame changes width. You haven't practiced width."

Jori said, "Good catch."

I hated praise during instruction.

"Brenna, frame. Olo, cloth."

Brenna looked at frame.

"Why me?"

"You already route around things you don't need to. I want see if you overprotect width."

"That's rude."

"Educational."

She took it.

Mett moved first.

Fine until bowl blocked low glow mark when held naturally.

He leaned sideways to find it.

"Stop," I said.

He froze.

Good.

"What do you know?"

"Wing post behind."

"Next boundary?"

"Center seam."

"Can you find without mark?"

He shifted foot carefully.

"Floor seam."

"Use it."

He did.

No drama.

Brenna with frame did exactly what predicted.

She kept staring at frame corner.

Not route.

"You're escorting object," I said.

"I don't want hit anything."

"Then know where you are. Object comes with you."

"Easy for you to say."

"I bring two long objects everywhere."

Pause.

Mett laughed first.

Brenna looked at crutches.

"Fine. Annoyingly fair."

She reset.

Second try better.

Olo with rolled cloth moved cleanly until Nessa's hood shifted slightly.

Light angle changed.

One glow tab became weaker.

He stopped.

Immediately.

No guess.

Good.

"What happened?" I asked.

"Mark changed."

"What do you do?"

"Stop. Find room."

"Do it."

He did.

There.

Teaching was mostly waiting for someone to make correct mistake.

Third round I added communication.

Not surprise obstacles.

Known obstruction.

A low empty crate placed partly across route.

Everyone saw it under full light first.

Then Nessa dimmed room.

"You're not testing memory of crate," I said. "You're practicing what happens when route isn't clear. First person finds it. What do you say?"

Mett said, "Crate."

"Where?"

"In way."

"Where?"

"Middle."

"Middle of what?"

He sighed deeply.

"Route between wing post and center seam, low obstruction, right half blocked."

"Good."

"That was many words."

"Fewer than ambulance."

Jori said, "We don't call it that."

"Whatever Carrow calls carrying idiot to healer."

Brenna said, "Stretcher team."

"Fewer than stretcher team."

Mett nodded.

"Less punchy."

They practiced.

Brenna's report was best.

Olo's too short.

"Low block, right."

"Which segment?"

"Wing to center."

"Good."

Then Mett tried to be helpful and moved crate in dark.

I heard scrape.

"Stop."

He froze.

"What?"

"Who told you move it?"

"Nobody."

"Then don't change map everyone else is using."

That landed.

Jori said, "Again."

Mett said, "I was fixing it."

Jori answered, "You were creating new condition without telling anyone."

Different voice from mine.

Authority.

Good.

We reset.

No punishment.

Again.

After an hour my throat hurt more than hands.

Unexpected occupational hazard.

We took break.

Nessa raised lamps halfway.

Mett sat on floor.

Brenna leaned against frame.

Olo remained standing.

I drank water Jori gave me.

Mett said, "So how do you do stairs?"

Not malicious.

Curious.

"Carefully."

"No, I mean with both crutches."

"Depends stairs. Rail changes everything."

"No rail?"

"Up or down?"

"Both."

"You want second course."

He grinned.

Brenna said, "Don't ask him. We'll be here all day."

"I thought he liked talking."

"He likes asking questions. Different disease."

I pointed at her.

"You learned quickly."

Olo said, "Why did Jori pick you?"

Direct.

I looked at him.

"She said because I think about route before moving."

"Because leg?"

"Partly."

He nodded.

No discomfort.

"Makes sense."

Then drank water.

That was entire conversation.

I liked him more.

Second hour we made routes less verbal.

Full spoken boundary every move was training scaffold, not actual backstage behavior.

Jori wanted short calls.

We settled on three useful ones already close to theatre language:

HOLD.

BLOCK.

CLEAR.

Jori owned exact meanings.

HOLD meant stop movement, keep position.

BLOCK meant route segment obstructed, followed by location.

CLEAR meant stated segment checked and open, not whole room safe forever.

I did not invent theatre vocabulary.

Important.

We practiced pairs.

One moved.

One watched route from fixed point.

Then swapped.

I became instructor instead of participant.

Strange.

First life had taught thousands of things.

Sword grip.

Mana circulation.

Field dressing.

How to sleep in wet armor.

How to identify wyvern spoor before breakfast.

How to tell young adventurer that bravery was not substitute for map.

I had trained recruits who later became captains.

Some died anyway.

Most teaching did not make people immortal.

It just removed stupid deaths from pile.

That was enough.

Mett rushed once.

I stopped him.

Brenna overcalled obstruction once.

Jori corrected.

Olo lost mark and stopped correctly twice.

Second time he found wing post by sound of Nessa adjusting lamp hood.

"No," I said.

He frowned.

"Why?"

"Nessa moves. Post doesn't."

He considered.

"Right."

"Use fixed boundary."

He did.

Good.

Near end Jori said, "One clean sequence. Then done."

Nessa lowered light.

Mett carried bowl.

Brenna carried frame.

Olo cloth.

Known crate obstruction remained.

No surprises.

Mett reached first segment.

Stopped when bowl hid mark.

Found floor seam.

Moved.

"BLOCK. Wing-center, right half."

Brenna answered from behind.

"HOLD."

Mett held.

Brenna repositioned frame before entering segment, keeping width inside left half.

"CLEAR left."

She crossed.

Olo waited.

Not because told.

Because route occupied.

Then moved after Brenna cleared.

His weak mark disappeared under changed angle again.

He stopped.

Looked around room, not mark.

Found rear rail.

Continued.

No collision.

No dropped prop.

No speed.

Boring.

Beautiful.

Nessa raised lights.

Mett said, "That's it?"

Jori said, "That's it."

"I expected something harder at end."

"Why?"

"Training always has hard thing at end."

I said, "Real work is hard thing. Training should make it less stupid."

Brenna nodded.

"I like that."

"Don't. I may charge."

Olo said, "You already are."

I stared at him.

Mett laughed loud enough to echo.

Olo almost smiled.

Dangerous.

Jori dismissed them.

Mett left talking about food.

Brenna reminded him he owed her something from yesterday.

Olo carried practice cloth back without being asked.

Jori waited until door shut.

"Good."

"Cala says that."

"She sounds wise."

"Terrifying."

Jori handed me two copper.

Actual coins.

I counted.

Two.

No bits.

Blessed simplicity.

Cash ten.

"If we do this again," Jori said, "I want you and Nessa to build one route drill for prop changes."

I looked at her.

"Does work exist?"

She smiled.

"Not yet."

"Then ask when it exists."

"I knew you'd say that."

"Why waste both our time?"

"Because sometimes people enjoy future planning."

"Unhealthy."

Nessa called from lamp.

"I still dislike him."

Jori said, "Noted."

I left theatre with ten copper and sore throat.

Rain had stopped.

Street smelled washed.

I took long route home for no reason except Lantern Court had apparently damaged me.

At one corner two delivery boys were trying to carry a narrow table through door sideways.

One said, "Lift your end."

Other said, "I am lifting."

They hit frame.

I kept walking.

Not instructor everywhere.

Important boundary.

At home Lyssa had brown carry-wrap pieces spread over table.

First lot still in progress.

Cala had moved dinner preparation to side counter.

Tavi sat under table doing something with string that looked illegal but probably wasn't.

Lyssa looked up.

"How was teaching?"

"No one died."

"High standard."

"They improved."

"Higher standard."

I put two copper with my money upstairs before dinner.

Ten.

Vale twenty-three.

For first time in a while, ten copper did not feel like fortune.

It felt like room.

Not enough for everything.

Enough that next interesting object could be a decision instead of joke.

Dangerous thought.

I wrote:

CASH: 10 C

VALE: 23 C

THEATRE ROUTE SESSION: +2 C

Then below:

START POINT

NEXT FIXED BOUNDARY

STOP CONDITION

DO NOT MOVE OBSTRUCTION WITHOUT CALL

I almost wrote more.

Didn't need to.

Teaching had reminded me of something old.

Not technique.

Role.

Instructor.

First life, I had worn it so long I stopped noticing.

People came because I knew more.

Sometimes because rank required them.

Sometimes because they were afraid.

Sometimes because they wanted to survive.

Today three stagehands had come because Jori paid me two copper and told them to.

Less majestic.

Probably healthier.

I closed notebook.

Instructor.

Still knew how.
# CHAPTER 368

## THE BIDDER

I learned about the auction because Sella said, "You like bad objects."

This was slander.

Accurate slander remained slander.

We met on South Cut by accident.

Actual accident.

No bridge rising.

No ropes snapping.

No one needed evacuation.

Sella stood beside a tea cart with one hand around clay cup and the other holding folded notice.

She saw me.

Looked at notice.

Looked back at me.

"You like bad objects."

"I like misunderstood objects."

"Same disease with better coat."

"What's notice?"

She handed it over.

CITY RECOVERY SALE

NORTH WEIGH YARD

SECOND BELL TOMORROW

UNCLAIMED / RETIRED / DAMAGED SERVICE GOODS

INSPECTION FROM FIRST BELL

NO POWERED TESTING ON SALE FLOOR

SOLD AS MARKED

BUYER REMOVES SAME DAY

Below that were lot families.

Hand tools.

Office fixtures.

Lamp housings.

Counterweights.

Route markers.

Kitchen service goods.

Two lines marked SPECIAL HANDLING.

No individual lots.

My pulse did something embarrassing.

Sella drank tea.

"There."

"What?"

"Face."

"I have face."

"Object face."

Apparently everyone had taxonomy for me now.

"Why aren't you going?"

"Because I work for living."

"Cruel."

"Also most recovery sale is junk."

"Most."

"Greg."

I folded notice.

"What does sold as marked mean here?"

"Whatever condition card says is what yard represents. They don't promise hidden function, remaining service life, compatibility, or repair cost. If card says cracked housing, you bought cracked housing. If card says retired, you bought retired."

"Inspection handling?"

"Usually yes unless red cord. No activation. No disassembly."

"Deposit?"

"No bidder deposit for public lots under silver threshold. Pay immediately if you win."

"Cash only?"

"Copper, silver, registered yard credit."

I had copper.

Ten.

Ten suddenly became less like room and more like loaded weapon.

Sella took notice back, then stopped.

"You want it?"

"Yes."

She gave it to me.

"Don't buy counterweight because it looks lonely."

"I have standards."

"You bought retired rest stone."

"It had history."

"Disease."

She walked away.

I stood there reading notice again.

No individual lots.

No guarantee anything interesting existed.

Could go and buy nothing.

Healthy people did that.

I knew several.

Probably.

At home Cala read notice once.

"Same-day removal."

Of course she found storage line first.

"Yes."

"Chest is not bigger because you have ten copper."

"I know."

Lyssa was stitching sleeve guard at table.

She didn't look up.

"Do you?"

"Hostile household."

"Storage household."

Tavi asked, "Can I come?"

Three adults said no.

He looked betrayed by democracy.

I set notice beside plate.

"I'm only inspecting."

Lyssa looked up now.

"That's worse sentence than 'I'm only looking.'"

"Inspection is more disciplined."

"You bought lantern after looking."

"Shade unit."

"See?"

Cala said, "If you buy something large, it doesn't come upstairs until we know where it goes."

Fair.

"Agreed."

"If it leaks?"

"I don't buy leaking."

"If seller says it doesn't leak?"

"I still inspect for leaking."

"If it starts leaking later?"

"Why is everything leaking?"

"Because you buy old magic."

Also fair.

I slept badly.

Not from worry.

Worse.

Anticipation.

First bell next morning I was at North Weigh Yard.

Healthy.

Normal.

North Weigh sat behind freight scales where stone lanes widened around roofed sheds.

Recovery sale occupied Shed Four.

A board at entrance repeated rules.

A clerk gave each bidder flat wooden paddle with painted number after name entry.

Mine was thirty-two.

No fee.

No bidder deposit.

"Payment due at lot close," clerk said. "Removal by sunset. Red-cord goods handled only by yard staff. Questions to floor clerks. Condition cards control."

"Can I withdraw bid before close?"

She looked at me like I had asked whether gravity negotiable.

"No."

Good rule to know.

Inside smelled like dust, iron, wet rope, old wood, lamp oil, and a little ozone.

There were maybe sixty lots.

Most were boring.

Beautifully boring.

Bent hooks.

Cracked wash basins.

Three bundles of mismatched shelf brackets.

A brass office bell with no striker.

Two hand lamps missing shutters.

A box of route tabs whose glow had faded to weak green.

A kitchen warming plate with one corner warped.

I walked everything once before touching anything.

First-life habit.

Auction rooms punished love at first sight.

Especially when love had condition card.

Lot twelve interested me.

RETIRED WALL INDEXER

MANUAL ROTATION FREE

MARKING CORE REMOVED

FRAME TRUE AT INTAKE

MOUNT PLATE INCLUDED

Six copper opening estimate written smaller below.

Without marking core it was furniture with ambition.

Passed.

Lot seventeen was red-cord.

A squat iron cylinder in wood cradle.

SERVICE PRESSURE RESERVOIR

RETIRED AFTER SEAL DRIFT

RESIDUAL CHARGE CLEARED AT INTAKE

DO NOT OPEN ON SALE FLOOR

Opening estimate four copper.

Absolutely not.

I loved it.

Absolutely not.

Growth.

Lot twenty-three was a set of three counterweight shoes.

Sella's voice entered brain.

Don't buy counterweight because it looks lonely.

I moved on out of spite.

Then lot thirty-one stopped me.

Small.

Good start.

Wooden case about length of forearm, shallow, with brass corners and two leather loops on back.

Inside, under lifted lid, sat six narrow ceramic slats arranged like ribs.

Not instrument.

Each slat had a blackened metal tongue at one end and faded number scratched near other.

Condition card:

LOT 31

RETIRED DRAFT-FINDER ARRAY

FORMER USE: WEST ARCHIVE STACKS

SIX OF EIGHT VANES PRESENT

TWO MISSING

CASE HINGE REPAIRED

PASSIVE RESPONSE OBSERVED AT INTAKE

CALIBRATION UNKNOWN

MOUNT STRAPS HARDENED

NO POWERED TESTING

No price estimate.

Interesting.

Draft finder.

Passive response.

Archive stacks.

Missing two of eight.

Not magic treasure.

Probably old environmental tool.

I looked for floor clerk.

Woman in orange sash approached.

"Question?"

"What does passive response observed mean on this card?"

"Intake clerk saw vane movement in airflow without activation source. That's all."

"Mana component?"

"Unknown. Former registry lists draft-finder array. Yard did not open tongues or test calibration."

"Why retired?"

She checked secondary tag hanging under card.

"Archive replacement cycle. Unit marked incomplete at removal. No fault code transferred."

"Can I lift case?"

"Yes. Don't remove vanes."

I lifted.

Maybe four pounds.

Fine.

Back loops could hang from wall or strap to frame.

I tilted slightly.

Ceramic slats barely moved.

No obvious loose rattle.

I set it down.

"Any compatible replacement vanes in sale?"

"Not listed as compatible."

Good answer.

"Thank you."

She moved on.

I stared.

What did I need draft finder for?

Nothing.

House had windows.

Theatre had smoke strips and professionals.

Travel maybe.

Bad answer.

Artifact desire liked to invent future selves.

I walked away.

Lot thirty-eight was better in obvious way.

A compact folding brazier with intact heat plate.

Condition card said serviceable manually, heat rune removed, ordinary charcoal use only.

Opening estimate two copper.

Useful.

Boring.

Could actually use.

We already had stove.

Passed.

Lot forty-four made me stop longer.

PAIR OF ROUTE ECHO PINS

RETIRED MUNICIPAL SURVEY

ONE RETURNS CLEAN TONE AT INTAKE

ONE RETURNS INTERMITTENT TONE

RANGE / PAIRING / CALIBRATION UNKNOWN

NO FIELD TEST

Two iron pegs with blue glass heads.

Potentially useful.

Potentially broken.

Potentially exactly kind of object that consumed three weeks and then taught me I owned two pegs.

I asked price expectation.

Floor clerk said no estimate.

I walked away.

That hurt.

Good.

At second bell auction started.

Not theatrical.

A yard caller stood on crate with clerk beside him.

Lots moved fast.

One through ten mostly sold for bits and low copper.

I did not bid.

Lot twelve wall indexer opened at four copper despite six estimate.

Two office furnishers fought to seven.

Visible salvage value.

Reasonable.

Lot seventeen pressure reservoir opened three.

A repair shop bidder took it at five.

Also reasonable.

They could service seals.

I could stare at seals.

Lot twenty-three counterweight shoes sold two copper to freight man.

I felt nothing.

Mostly.

Lot thirty-one arrived.

"Retired draft-finder array," caller said. "Six of eight vanes. Passive response observed. Calibration unknown. West Archive former service. Opening one copper."

One copper.

My paddle moved before brain approved.

"One, thirty-two."

Another paddle lifted.

"Two, fourteen."

Bidder fourteen was older woman with ink-stained fingers.

Maybe archivist.

Maybe collector.

Maybe murderer.

Irrelevant.

Two copper.

At two, object was still interesting.

At three?

I had ten.

Three left seven.

Vale twenty-three unchanged.

Could pay debt instead.

Could keep reserve.

Could buy actual food/tools later.

Draft finder did not solve current problem.

Paddle fourteen stayed up.

Caller looked around.

"Two copper. Any three?"

I raised.

"Three, thirty-two."

Woman fourteen looked at me.

Not hostile.

Assessing.

Raised.

"Four, fourteen."

Four.

This was where auctions became confession.

What did I believe object worth to me?

Not hidden market value.

Not theoretical magic.

To me.

Four copper was forty percent of liquid cash.

For incomplete unknown-calibration passive environmental instrument.

No.

I lowered paddle.

Caller waited.

"Four copper. Once. Twice. Sold fourteen."

Pain.

Clean pain.

Good pain.

Woman fourteen won draft finder.

I still had ten copper.

This was success.

I hated success.

Lot thirty-eight brazier sold three.

I did not bid.

Lot forty-four.

Echo pins.

Caller read card.

"Opening one copper."

No paddles.

Interesting.

"One copper?"

Still none.

My brain started inventing.

One clean tone.

One intermittent.

Municipal survey.

Could maybe establish direction or paired route response.

Could maybe be useless without missing receiver.

Card said pair.

Former pair, maybe.

Unknown pairing/calibration.

One copper was cheap because obvious condition bad and use uncertain.

This was exactly where information gap could exist.

Also exactly where garbage lived.

I raised paddle.

"One, thirty-two."

Caller looked.

"Two?"

A man near rear lifted paddle.

"Two, forty-one."

Of course.

He wore surveyer's gray vest.

Actual likely user.

Bad sign for bargain.

Good sign for object relevance.

I looked at pins.

Two copper.

Could justify.

Maybe.

I raised three.

"Three, thirty-two."

Survey man raised four immediately.

No hesitation.

There.

He knew something or had compatible equipment.

Either way market signal.

Four.

Would I go five?

Half cash.

For one intermittent retired pin pair with unknown range/calibration.

No.

Paddle down.

"Four, forty-one. Once. Twice. Sold."

Second loss.

Strangely easier.

Because bidder made sense.

Market wasn't asleep waiting for me.

Good.

Auction continued.

I almost left.

Then lot fifty-two appeared.

Not artifact.

At least not obviously.

A narrow leather carrying harness with two adjustable side loops and broad back strap.

Condition card:

PORTER'S SIDE HARNESS

USED

STITCHING SOUND

ONE BUCKLE REPLACED

NO LOAD RATING REPRESENTED

Opening one copper.

I stared.

This was mundane.

Potentially useful.

Side loops could carry long object against torso while leaving hands free.

Crutches occupied hands.

Shoulder bag already did some of this badly.

Could carry cloth.

Could carry narrow cases.

Could maybe carry Three Reeds if padded, though artifact storage rules screamed.

Could carry groceries.

Could carry nothing and become expensive belt.

One copper.

No one bid.

I raised paddle.

"One, thirty-two."

Silence.

"Any two?"

A porter near front inspected it from seat.

Did not bid.

That mattered.

Maybe because used.

Maybe because no rating.

Maybe because he had better.

Caller said, "One once. One twice. Sold thirty-two."

I had bought harness.

Not magic.

I felt betrayed.

Payment clerk took one copper.

Cash nine.

She gave receipt and lot release tag.

I carried harness to inspection bench before leaving.

Same orange-sash clerk watched while I checked stitching more closely.

No hidden cuts.

Replacement buckle mismatched brass.

Leather dry but not cracked through.

"Can I put it on empty?"

"Yes."

I did.

Awkward with crutches.

Clerk held one strap only after I asked.

Harness sat diagonally across back/side.

One loop landed too low near left hip.

Adjustable.

I shortened.

Better.

Right side could hold narrow bundle without interfering with right crutch if object stayed behind elbow line.

Left side more complicated because residual limb and crutch path.

Could still use one-sided.

No load rating.

Important.

Not for heavy objects until someone competent checked it.

I removed.

"Do you know maker?"

Clerk looked at worn stamp.

"Looks like Heddel porter goods. Old mark. Could be copy."

"Any shop still services?"

"Heddel shop closed years ago. Leatherworker can assess stitching. Buckle standard enough."

Good.

No magical secret.

Just tool.

I left with harness over shoulder and nine copper.

Outside, bidder fourteen was loading draft-finder case into small handcart.

I tried not to look.

Failed.

She noticed.

"You wanted it."

"At three."

She smiled.

"At four too."

"Apparently not."

"Good."

I looked at her.

She tapped case.

"I'm buying six vanes, not array."

There.

Information.

"Replacement stock?"

"Maybe. Same ceramic profile as old archive humidity shutters. If tongues are wrong, I bought six pretty strips."

"You knew profile before bidding?"

"I could see it."

Fair.

"West Archive?"

"My father serviced stacks twenty years."

More information.

Market rational.

She looked at harness.

"You bought strap."

"Apparently."

"Useful."

"Less exciting."

"Useful often is."

She pushed cart away.

No name.

No subplot.

Just person who beat me because she knew more.

Excellent.

Survey man with echo pins passed next.

He didn't stop.

One pin in hand already.

He flicked glass head with fingernail.

It gave faint clear tone.

Other answered from box at his hip.

Not the second sale pin.

Compatible equipment.

Of course.

Four copper made even more sense.

I laughed.

He glanced back.

Kept walking.

At home Cala saw harness.

Looked behind me.

"That's all?"

"You sound disappointed."

"I'm checking for cylinder."

"There was cylinder."

Her face changed.

"Greg."

"I did not buy cylinder."

"Good."

Lyssa was at table again.

She held out hand.

"Give me harness."

"Why?"

"Because I sew."

Good reason.

I handed it over.

She bent leather.

Checked stitching.

Pulled replacement buckle.

"Dry."

"Not cracked through."

"Yet."

"Clerk said leatherworker assessment before load."

She nodded.

"One copper?"

"One."

"That's fine."

I felt absurdly pleased.

"I lost two auctions first."

"You didn't lose."

"They bought objects I wanted."

"Did you bid more than you wanted to pay?"

"No."

"Then you didn't lose."

I hated when people used my own logic against me.

Tavi came in.

"What is it?"

"Harness."

"Magic?"

"No."

He lost interest instantly.

Children were honest markets.

Later I took harness to leatherworker Cala knew two streets west.

Not a named recurring character.

He charged no inspection fee because it took less than minute and I did not ask him to repair.

"Stitching's fine for light carry," he said. "Leather wants oil. Don't trust that replacement buckle over maybe ten, twelve pounds until pin changed. Side loops weren't for heavy freight anyway. Documents, tools, narrow parcels."

"Can you replace pin?"

"Yes. Not today."

"Cost?"

"Depends pin. Come back if you care."

I cared later.

Not today.

At home I oiled leather with Cala's permission and cloth she gave me.

No artifact test.

No hidden glow.

No ancient rune appearing under dirt.

Leather became slightly darker.

That was all.

I tried harness empty again.

Then with rolled blanket.

Light.

Bulky enough to test geometry.

Right-side carry worked better than shoulder-bag strap improvisation.

Weight sat lower and closer to torso.

Crutch path clear if loop shortened.

Left-side carry interfered with left crutch during longer swing.

So one-sided.

Useful constraint.

I wrote:

CASH: 9 C

VALE: 23 C

RECOVERY SALE

DRAFT FINDER: STOPPED AT 3 / SOLD 4

ECHO PINS: STOPPED AT 3 / SOLD 4

PORTER HARNESS: 1 C

LIGHT CARRY ONLY UNTIL BUCKLE PIN CHECKED

RIGHT SIDE BETTER

Then I stared at first two lines.

Stopped at three.

Twice.

That felt better than buying either.

Not because objects were bad.

Draft finder might be excellent for woman who knew its vanes.

Echo pins were clearly worth more to man with compatible equipment.

Value was not inside object alone.

It lived between object and owner.

Dangerous sentence.

Sounded like philosophy.

I crossed it out before writing it.

No need.

I had nine copper, one useful harness, and no mysterious pressure cylinder leaking in bedroom.

Bidder.

Apparently restraint counted too.
# CHAPTER 369

## THE CARRIER

The harness became useful because Lyssa made too much cloth.

Not personally.

That would have been alarming.

She had finished Marra's first lot.

Twelve aprons.

Twelve sleeve pairs.

Eight carry wraps.

"One."

One bundle.

Not the largest.

Better.

Of course.

"No."

FIRST LOT

6 C

2 B BENCH

ABOUT 2.5 DAYS WORK

3-STITCH FIX

MARra ERROR ON WRAPS

9 C

BIGGER

5 DAYS

NO BENCH INCLUDED

DO I WANT TO DO THIS EVERY WEEK?

Too much.

Messy phrase.

Good phrase.

Not her nine maybe.

CASH: 9 C

VALE: 23 C

PORTER HARNESS

RIGHT-SIDE LIGHT PARCEL: WORKS

Did not.

Not my ledger.

Still mattered.

That was inconvenient.

Some of best things happening in my life refused to become my property, income, skill, or problem.

I was getting better at letting that happen.

Maybe.

Carrier.

Today that had been enough.

"It works."

Attempt six failed because I reproduced it.

I swore.

Hessa did not smile.

Her eyes did.

Attempt seven.

Nothing.

Eight.

Bead moved, but wind line had started shifting just before effect.

Hessa said, "Discard."

"It moved before big gust."

"Discard."

"You enjoy waste."

"I enjoy not lying."

Fair.

Attempt eight still counted as attempt.

Result discarded as evidence.

Nine.

No effect.

Ten.

Tiny clean movement.

Not as much as five.

But timing clean.

No wind jump.

No late shoulder.

Hessa raised hand.

Stop.

"That is ten," I said.

"Yes."

"You said twelve."

"I changed mind."

"There are two left."

"No."

"Why?"

"Because I have two clean-enough farther results and you are beginning to chase success."

I opened mouth.

Closed.

She was right.

Worse.

"So ten counted farther attempts."

"Yes."

"Two clean enough."

"Yes."

"One other moved late. One moved under wind noise and gets discarded as evidence."

"Yes."

"Four baseline attempts first, one clean enough."

"Yes."

"External total becomes one hundred twenty-nine."

Hessa paused.

I counted again.

One hundred fifteen before today.

Four near baseline.

Ten farther.

Fourteen.

One hundred twenty-nine.

"Correct," she said.

"Minimal fifty-nine. Shaping fifty-three."

"Correct."

I leaned on crutches.

Not exhausted.

Hands slightly warm from route repetition.

Shoulders working.

Brain louder.

"So distance improved."

Hessa looked at me.

I sighed.

"No."

"Try again."

"Today, on this route, after familiarization, I produced two clean-enough small external effects on a stationary target about one pace farther than prior near-range moving-caster work. Two out of ten counted farther attempts."

"Better."

"One clean baseline out of four at old distance."

"Yes."

"Which means I was not especially reliable even before distance changed."

"Yes."

"You could say something encouraging."

"You noticed."

That was apparently encouragement.

I sat on dry trough edge.

Hessa gave me water.

I drank.

Overhead tabs fluttered.

"Why this yard?" I asked.

"Available."

I stared.

"That's all?"

"No."

Of course.

She pointed to tabs.

"South Walk is too clean."

There.

"You wanted environmental noise visible."

"Some."

"But not moving target."

"Correct."

"And route has turns so I cannot make one perfect straight-line timing ritual."

"Partly."

"What else?"

"You tell me."

Trap.

I looked at court.

Three troughs.

Narrow posts.

Rough seam.

Broad return.

Target farther.

Wind visible.

No crowd.

No real consequence if effect failed.

"It makes me move like I actually move. Not marching lane."

Hessa nodded once.

"Closer."

"Current body route changes. Crutch placement changes with width and surface. You want effect to survive some ordinary geometry without adding target movement or speed increase yet."

"Yes."

There.

I felt pleased.

Hessa ruined it.

"But I did not count that as separate variable."

"Why not?"

"Because today is not proof of route-general skill. You learned this loop first."

Right.

"So this is still one practiced route."

"Yes."

"Just less artificial than South Walk."

"Yes."

"You are deeply committed to making every result smaller."

"Small results fit through doors."

That sounded like something Hessa had been waiting years to say.

"Was that metaphor?"

"No."

"It was."

"Drink water."

I drank.

She packed bead.

I watched hands.

Young hands.

Competent.

That still did something strange to me sometimes.

Not because Hessa was young exactly.

I was young now too.

That remained rude.

In first life I had taught people older than her.

Fought beside people younger.

Taken orders from specialists who knew things I didn't.

Age had never made expertise simple.

But being nineteen again put old reflex in wrong room.

I wanted to skip explanation because I remembered categories.

Wanted to infer next drill because I knew training structures.

Wanted to turn every correction into system before system had enough evidence.

Hessa kept making me do stupid thing instead.

Be student.

Not pretend ignorance.

Not erase first life.

Just let somebody else own lesson when it was theirs.

Annoying.

Probably useful.

"Why are you making face?" Hessa asked.

"Personal growth."

"Stop."

Reasonable.

She closed case.

"No independent moving external work."

"Yes."

"No farther target practice alone."

"Yes."

"No artifact combination."

"Yes."

"No using Three Reeds to create controlled visual field for casting."

I looked at her.

"I hadn't thought of that."

"Now you have."

"This is your fault."

"Still no."

"Cruel."

"Useful."

We left dye yard.

At gate I asked, "Next axis speed?"

Hessa kept walking.

"Maybe."

"Distance again?"

"Maybe."

"Stationary casting at farther range to separate movement cost?"

She looked at me.

That one apparently less stupid.

"Maybe."

"You have three maybes."

"I have more."

"Can I have one?"

"No."

Teacher.

Terrible species.

We split near East Cloth.

Hessa went north without goodbye.

I went toward Marra's green door because Lyssa had said she was answering after breakfast.

Not to supervise.

Mostly because route home passed within half block.

I saw her before I reached door.

She came out carrying one folded work card and no cloth.

"You took it," I said.

"I said I would."

"You said you thought you would."

"Now I did."

"Nine copper. Five days."

"Yes."

"Same categories?"

She gave me look.

I stopped.

"Sorry."

"Thank you."

We walked together.

After ten steps she said, "Yes, same categories. Marra wrote client-update line onto card this time."

"Good."

"I know."

"Any wrap rework?"

"Hall accepts visible patch line. Marra offered me one copper to move all eight loops. I said yes. Separate from second lot. I can do it this afternoon."

There.

New money.

Her money.

New work.

Her work.

"Good," I said.

She pointed at me without looking.

"One good. That's all."

"Understood."

"How was magic?"

"Hessa made me student."

"Were you not already?"

"Hostile question."

"Did anything move?"

"Yes."

"That sounds good."

"Careful. Hessa might hear."

Lyssa looked around.

"Is she in wall?"

"Tavi believes possible."

"Then definitely."

At home Tavi had cleaned cabinet doors.

Mostly.

One had a wet streak shaped like hand.

Cala inspected.

"You missed top left."

Tavi looked at chair.

Then at me.

Then at Lyssa.

"Can someone tall do it?"

I pointed at him.

"Learning."

Cala handed cloth to Lyssa.

Lyssa wiped top left in two seconds.

Tavi looked offended by efficiency.

"I could've done that."

"You did rest," Cala said.

"Most."

"Most is why we're here."

He accepted this with visible reluctance.

I went upstairs.

No money movement for me.

Nine copper.

Twenty-three Vale.

I wrote:

59 MINIMAL

53 DELIBERATE SHAPING

129 EXTERNAL EFFECT

MOVING CASTER / PRACTICED LOOP / STATIONARY TARGET

OLD NEAR RANGE: 4 ATTEMPTS / 1 CLEAN ENOUGH

FARTHER BY ABOUT 1 PACE: 10 COUNTED ATTEMPTS / 2 CLEAN ENOUGH

1 LATE MOVEMENT

1 MOVEMENT UNDER WIND NOISE: DISCARD AS EVIDENCE

WIND-JUMP PASSES SKIPPED / NOT COUNTED

Then:

DO NOT GENERALIZE TO MOVING TARGET / FASTER ROUTE / UNFAMILIAR ROUTE / UNSUPERVISED USE

Then I almost wrote:

I KNOW WHAT HESSA IS DOING.

I stopped.

Crossed blank space where sentence would have gone.

That was old habit.

Knowing shape of lesson before lesson finished.

Sometimes useful.

Sometimes just another way of trying to stand where teacher stood.

I wrote instead:

NEXT: HESSA DECIDES.

Stared at it.

Hated it.

Left it.

Student.

Apparently restraint counted there too.
